claim: The background legacy writes derive their context from the request ctx, which net/http cancels when the handler returns, so the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection can be aborted before they run.
body:
## [RACE CONDITION] Async legacy write inherits the request context and is cancelled when the handler returns

**Severity:** HIGH — async legacy writes can be cancelled as soon as the request returns

### The Problem
```go
go func() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))
```
`ctx` here is the incoming request context. The same pattern is used at lines 110, 135 and 163. `context.WithTimeoutCause` derives a child context, so a cancelled parent cancels the child straight away. The 10s timeout only makes the deadline shorter. It never makes it longer.

### Theory / Proof
The `net/http` docs for `Request.Context` say: "For incoming server requests, the context is canceled when the client's connection closes, the request is canceled (with HTTP/2), or when the ServeHTTP method returns." Mode 3 returns `created` to the handler right away, the response is written, and ServeHTTP returns. From that point the goroutine's context is Done. The legacy SQL store passes ctx down to the DB session, so the write fails with `context canceled` or never starts.

### What happens today vs. what will break
Unit tests pass because they use `context.Background()`, which is never cancelled. In a real server the legacy write races the response. On a fast path the goroutine may finish first. Under load it will often lose, and legacy quietly falls behind unified storage. That defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ("write to legacy, just as a safe measure"). Rolling back to mode 1/2 would then expose stale data.

### Research
Go 1.21 added `context.WithoutCancel` for exactly this case: work that must outlive the request but still needs its values (auth identity, namespace, logger). Kubernetes and other Go servers use it, or a detached context, for post-response work. Mode 1 in this package has the same pattern, so it should be fixed there as well.

### Recommendation
```go
go func() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), 10*time.Second, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))
    defer cancel()
    ...
}()
```
Apply the same change to Delete, Update and DeleteCollection.

claim: Update passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update, so legacy recomputes the new object against its own old object instead of receiving the object unified storage persisted; the previous updateWrapper that guaranteed identical content was removed.
body:
## [ISSUE] Legacy Update recomputes the object instead of writing what unified storage stored

**Severity:** MEDIUM — legacy may end up with different content than unified storage

### The Problem
```go
_, _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, objInfo, createValidation, updateValidation, forceAllowCreate, options)
```
The old code wrapped the result of the unified update in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`. That made `UpdatedObject` return the exact object written to unified storage (see `dualwriter.go:128-144`). The new code passes the original `objInfo`, so the legacy store calls `objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, legacyOld)` itself.

### Theory / Proof
For PATCH requests, the apiserver's `objInfo` applies the patch to whatever old object it is given and runs admission again. Legacy's old object can differ from unified storage's. Mode 3 reads only from unified, and earlier async legacy writes may have failed. When that happens the patch gives a different result in legacy, or fails validation. `UpdatedObject` is also called a second time, outside the request, which repeats admission side effects.

### What happens today vs. what will break
A full PUT where both stores agree works fine. A PATCH, or any update after one missed legacy write, leaves legacy with different content, and the only sign is an error-flag histogram sample.

### Research
Mode 2 in this package (`dualwriter_mode2.go` Update) wraps the object persisted in the first store in `updateWrapper` before writing it to the second store. Mode 3 did the same before this PR.

### Recommendation
```go
go func(updated runtime.Object) {
    ...
    _, _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Update(ctx, name, &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: updated},
        createValidation, updateValidation, forceAllowCreate, options)
    ...
}(res.DeepCopyObject())
```

claim: Delete records the storage duration with the object name as the `kind` label, which creates one histogram series per deleted object.
body:
## [ISSUE] Delete records the object name as the `kind` metric label

**Severity:** MEDIUM — unbounded metric cardinality

### The Problem
```go
d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)
```
Every other call passes `options.Kind`. The third argument ends up in the `kind` label of `grafana_dual_writer_storage_duration_seconds` (`metrics.go`: labels `is_error, mode, kind, method`).

### Theory / Proof
Every Prometheus label combination is a separate time series. A native histogram (`NativeHistogramBucketFactor: 1.1`) per series costs a noticeable amount of memory. Object names are user-controlled and unbounded, so every successful delete of a distinct name adds a new series that is never garbage-collected.

### What happens today vs. what will break
Dashboards filtered by `kind` also miss every successful mode 3 delete. Over time the process's memory and scrape size grow with the number of distinct names deleted.

### Research
The Prometheus naming best practices say: "Do not use labels to store dimensions with high cardinality (many different label values), such as user IDs...". Mode 1 has the same bug at `dualwriter_mode1.go:155`, which looks like where it was copied from.

### Recommendation
```go
d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)
```

claim: Storage failures in Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) are recorded in the legacy histogram, and the async legacy DeleteCollection (line 166) is recorded in the storage histogram, so the two metrics used to judge migration health are wrong.
body:
## [ISSUE] Storage and legacy durations are recorded into the wrong histograms

**Severity:** MEDIUM — storage vs legacy metrics are misattributed

### The Problem
- Line 45: `Storage.Create` failed, but `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` is called.
- Line 129: `Storage.Update` failed, but `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` is called.
- Line 166: inside the goroutine that calls `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection`, `d.recordStorageDuration(...)` is called.

### Theory / Proof
`dual_writer_storage_duration_seconds` and `dual_writer_legacy_duration_seconds` are the only signals that tell operators whether the unified or legacy store is failing in mode 3. Legacy writes are fire-and-forget and never logged (see the goroutines), so the legacy `is_error=true` series is the only way to see legacy failures.

### What happens today vs. what will break
With the current code, a failing unified store shows up as legacy errors. A failing legacy DeleteCollection shows up as unified-storage errors and doubles the storage samples for delete-collection. Any alert or rollout decision based on these series will point at the wrong backend.

### Research
Mode 2 (`dualwriter_mode2.go`) consistently pairs each store call with its own record function.

### Recommendation
```go
// line 45 and line 129
d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)
// line 166
d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)
```

claim: Each write spawns an independent goroutine for legacy with no ordering and no error logging, so a quick create-then-update/delete on the same object can apply to legacy out of order, and failures leave no log trail.
body:
## [RACE CONDITION] Unordered, unlogged fire-and-forget legacy writes

**Severity:** MEDIUM — legacy can permanently diverge and failures are invisible

### The Problem
Create (line 50), Delete (108), Update (134) and DeleteCollection (161) each start a new goroutine. Nothing orders these goroutines per object, and the goroutines log nothing on error. They only record a histogram sample.

### Theory / Proof
Go does not guarantee any ordering between goroutines. Suppose a client creates `foo` and then deletes it immediately. Unified storage applies both in order, because each request waits for the synchronous storage write. The two legacy goroutines, though, can run in either order. If Delete runs first, it gets NotFound, then Create succeeds, and legacy is left with an object that unified storage does not have. The same thing happens with Create then Update, or two Updates, where the older value can win in legacy.

### What happens today vs. what will break
With low traffic and one write per object, ordering rarely matters. Automated clients (provisioning, GitOps, tests) that write the same object several times in a row will leave legacy in a different state from unified. Nothing logs it, and there is no name or error to reconcile from, so a rollback to mode 1/2 serves stale or resurrected objects.

### Research
Standard dual-write migrations (for example Stripe's online migration pattern, or outbox/CDC approaches) either keep the secondary write synchronous or serialize secondary writes per key and log failures for reconciliation.

### Recommendation
At minimum, log failures with the object name so they can be reconciled:
```go
if errObjectSt != nil {
    log.Error(errObjectSt, "unable to create object in legacy storage")
}
```
Also consider serializing legacy writes per object key, for example with a keyed mutex or a single worker per resource, or keeping the legacy write synchronous but non-fatal as the previous implementation did.

claim: Delete stores `d.Log` instead of the enriched `log` in the context, so downstream storage code logs without the name/kind/method fields every other method attaches.
body:
## [ISSUE] Delete puts the un-enriched logger into the context

**Severity:** LOW — delete path loses its structured log fields

### The Problem
```go
log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)
ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)
```
Every other method does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

### Theory / Proof
`klog.FromContext(ctx)` in the storage layers returns whatever logger was put into the context. Here that is the base logger without `name`, `kind` and `method`.

### What happens today vs. what will break
Logs still get written, but they cannot be correlated to the object being deleted.

### Research
Consistent with Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection in this same file.

### Recommendation
```go
ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)
```

claim: The goroutine passes the original `obj` to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has run on it, without DeepCopyObject, so legacy sees storage-assigned metadata and shares a mutable object with the returned response path.
body:
## [ISSUE] Legacy Create reuses the same `obj` pointer without a DeepCopy

**Severity:** MEDIUM — legacy receives an object already mutated by unified storage, with a possible data race

### The Problem
```go
created, err := d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, createValidation, options)
...
go func() {
    _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(ctx, obj, createValidation, options)
```

### Theory / Proof
The apiserver generic registry's `Store.Create` calls `rest.BeforeCreate` on the passed object. That fills in UID and creationTimestamp and runs `PrepareForCreate` in place. Some storage implementations also return the same pointer as `created`. After the handler returns, the response encoder reads `created` while the goroutine hands `obj` to legacy storage, which may convert or modify it. Two goroutines access the same object without synchronization, and `go test -race` flags that.

### What happens today vs. what will break
With the mocks, `obj` is never mutated, so the tests do not catch it. Mode 1 in this same package explicitly does `createdCopy := created.DeepCopyObject()` before handing the object to a goroutine (`dualwriter_mode1.go:51`). Mode 3 skips that.

### Research
Mode 1 (`dualwriter_mode1.go:51-53`) deep-copies the object before passing it to the async goroutine.

### Recommendation
```go
go func(createdCopy runtime.Object) {
    ...
    _, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(ctx, createdCopy, createValidation, options)
    ...
}(created.DeepCopyObject())
```

claim: Legacy and storage mocks share one mock.Mock, so the 'legacy' expectation in the create error case actually drives the Storage.Create failure, and no test ever asserts the async legacy write happened.
body:
## [GAP ANALYSIS] Shared mock hides which store is called; async legacy writes are untested

**Severity:** MEDIUM — tests do not verify what their names claim

### The Problem
```go
ls := legacyStoreMock{m, l}
us := storageMock{m, s}
```
Both wrappers record calls on the same `m`. In "error when creating object in the unified store fails", only `setupLegacyFn` registers `Create` returning an error. That expectation is what makes `Storage.Create` fail. The test calls it a legacy expectation, but it is exercising storage.

### Theory / Proof
testify's `mock.Mock` matches on method name and arguments only. It cannot tell apart two wrappers that share it. The goroutines also run after the test assertions, and there is no `m.AssertExpectations` or `Eventually`, so the tests would pass even if the legacy write were removed or given the wrong arguments.

### What happens today vs. what will break
Every async legacy behavior added in this PR (context use, metric labels, arguments passed to legacy) is untested. That is why the metric mislabeling and the object-name label shipped unnoticed.

### Research
testify recommends one mock per dependency and `AssertExpectations(t)`. For async calls, `assert.Eventually` or a channel signalled from `.Run(...)` is the usual pattern.

### Recommendation
Use separate mocks for legacy and storage, and wait for the async call:
```go
done := make(chan struct{})
lm.On("Create", mock.Anything, mock.Anything, mock.Anything, mock.Anything).
    Return(exampleObj, nil).Run(func(mock.Arguments) { close(done) })
...
select { case <-done: case <-time.After(time.Second): t.Fatal("legacy create not called") }
lm.AssertExpectations(t)
```
